speaker: Zach Perret
title: How Plaid Survived on K Before Becoming Fintech Infrastructure | Zach Perret
question: When AI tools make software engineers dramatically more productive, why don't high-growth tech startups simply cut headcount in half?
guest: I can't speak for all organizations, and I certainly can't speak for companies outside of Silicon Valley, because I don't know how the insides of an accounting firm or a law firm work, and there I do think there will be meaningful job changes. But in our business, and in all of the other startups that I know, if you can do more, you're going to do more. If you can afford to hire more people in order to do more, and the leverage that you get out of those people is dramatically larger, you're going to just build more stuff. You're going to create more products. You're going to add more value for your customers. So I think that the insatiable demand of doing more, building more, creating better products for your customers will continue, and I would expect that startup headcount will continue to grow. I can't speak for big companies, but certainly for us, if I can hire an engineer that's twice as efficient, that sounds great. That's a great deal. I should hire that engineer and then build products that generate far more value for the company.

points.core: Growth startups face insatiable demand to build additional products for customers.
points.note: Accept: unbounded product roadmaps or elastic appetite to ship more features and customer value. Do not credit: generic optimism that tech always grows without citing elastic product demand.

points.core: Higher per-engineer AI leverage makes hiring additional engineers a better financial deal.
points.note: Accept: hiring a twice-as-efficient engineer yields greater value per dollar, incentivizing continued hiring rather than cuts. Do not credit: vague claims that AI augments humans without explaining the improved hiring ROI.

points.core: Fixed-scope service firms face sharper headcount disruption than product-driven tech startups.
points.note: Accept: distinguishing traditional professional services (e.g., law or accounting firms) or mature enterprises from growth startups. Do not credit: claiming AI will never reduce headcount in any industry.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Because for a high-growth startup, engineering is not a fixed workload to be completed at minimum cost; it is the main constraint on how fast the company can grow. When each engineer becomes more productive, the return on hiring an engineer rises, so the rational move is usually to build more, not to employ fewer.

Several forces reinforce this. Startups have backlogs far larger than their capacity, so cheaper software unlocks features, products and experiments that previously weren't worth the cost; this is the Jevons paradox, where efficiency increases total demand. Competitors get the same tools, so a company that banks the gain as savings is out-shipped by rivals who reinvest it. Investors also value these companies on growth rather than margins, so cutting payroll buys little.

Finally, coding is only part of the job. AI speeds up writing code much more than it speeds up deciding what to build, system design, review, debugging, on-call and customer understanding, so those bottlenecks still need people.

Mature, slow-growth companies with bounded roadmaps face a different calculation, which is where headcount cuts are more likely.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
High-growth startups optimize for speed and market capture, not cost minimization against a fixed workload. Cutting headcount in half assumes a static backlog, whereas ambitious startups face virtually boundless opportunities to build new features, run product experiments, and expand into adjacent markets. Because demand for software is highly elastic—an effect akin to Jevons paradox—lowering the time and cost required to ship code raises the return on engineering, encouraging companies to build more rather than spend less.

Competitive pressure reinforces this calculus. If rival startups equip full-sized teams with AI to iterate twice as fast, shrinking your team simply to maintain yesterday's output means surrendering market share. Furthermore, typing code is only one fraction of software engineering. As AI accelerates implementation, bottlenecks shift toward human-intensive judgment: product discovery, system architecture, security, code review, and operational reliability, especially as larger volumes of AI-generated code enter production. Ultimately, AI turns each engineer into a higher-leverage asset, making it far more rational for growth-focused companies to double velocity than to halve payroll.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
High-growth startups are limited by opportunity, not by a fixed amount of work. Their main constraint is how fast they can capture a market before competitors do. When each engineer produces more, building a feature gets cheaper, and the startup can pursue more of them. This is the Jevons paradox: making something more efficient often increases total demand for it. The startup ships more products, runs more experiments, and moves into adjacent markets sooner. Cutting staff would save money, but it would give up growth, and investors usually value growth far more.

Competition also matters. Rivals have the same AI tools, so the productivity gain doesn't give anyone a lasting edge. A team that halves its headcount just falls behind a rival that kept everyone and moves twice as fast.

Finally, writing code was never the only bottleneck. Engineers also spend time on system design, judging what to build, debugging, reviewing AI-generated code, managing reliability and security, and working with customers. AI speeds up these tasks much less, so the gains are smaller than they look.

Mature companies chasing efficiency are the ones more likely to cut staff.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
High-growth startups rarely cut engineering headcount when AI boosts productivity because their goal isn't to minimize costs—it's to capture a market before competitors do. When writing code becomes cheaper and faster, demand for software actually expands, an effect economists call the Jevons paradox. Every startup sits on an enormous backlog of deferred features, integrations, reliability improvements, and new product lines that previously weren't worth the engineering hours. AI makes those projects suddenly viable, so keeping the same team lets a startup ship faster, outpace rivals, and expand into adjacent markets.

Moreover, generating code is only a fraction of software engineering. Faster code production shifts the bottleneck to system architecture, code review, security, testing, and deciding what to build in the first place—areas that still require experienced engineers. Cutting headcount in half would surrender a startup's speed advantage to competitors who instead use AI to multiply their existing teams' output.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Because a high-growth startup usually has more valuable work than its engineers can get to. If AI lets the same team ship faster, the company can launch features sooner, run more experiments, and respond faster to customers. When those gains are worth more than the payroll savings, keeping the team makes business sense.

Doubling coding speed also rarely doubles the team’s overall output. Engineers still have to figure out what to build, coordinate changes, review code, and keep the product running. As coding gets faster, one of those other tasks may become the bottleneck.

Startups can still use AI to slow hiring or cut roles when cash is tight or demand is weak. The decision comes down to how much the next engineer can contribute compared with what they cost. In a fast-growing company, AI can increase that contribution.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Cutting headcount in half makes sense if the goal is to ship the same product at lower cost. A high-growth startup usually has more ideas than it can pursue, so AI changes the calculation. If keeping the team lets the company launch a feature months earlier, win customers, or test which product is worth building, that can be worth more than the payroll savings.

Faster coding also doesn’t translate directly into a proportionally smaller team. Engineers still have to figure out what customers need, make design decisions, review changes, and keep systems running. Some startups will slow hiring or cut roles, especially when cash is tight. The deciding question is how much value the team can create with the time AI frees up.
